newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin aide slams NATO stance as unjust and wrong.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin aide slams NATO stance as unjust and wrong.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's foreign policy adviser on Tuesday denounced NATO's refusal to grant Russia a veto right on key isssues of European security as "strange, unjust and wrong", Interfax news agency said.
Dmitry Ryurikov, stepping up Moscow's war of words against NATO's plans to incorporate some former Warsaw Pact states, also said the expansion posed a direct military threat to Russia.

NATO has vowed to expand regardless of Russian misgivings but has offered Moscow "special relations" as compensation. Russia says this is not enough and wants a "binding agreement" that would effectively give it a right of veto.

"It is an extremely strange position," Interfax quoted Ryurikov as saying. He referred to "opinions expressed in the West over the impermissibility of granting Russia a veto right over issues concerning the safety of the continent."
"It is unjust and wrong," he said.
Ryurikov said there was a consensus in Russia over NATO's expansion plans and added this was a result of the "purely military threat" that it would imply.

Ryurikov said that a visit by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana to the former Soviet republics -- he was in Moldova on Monday and flew to Georgia on Tuesday -- "should be considered as a demonstration of NATO's tough position over its expansion".
Moscow is bitterly opposed to NATO expansion, arguing that it would threaten domestic security and could undermine Yeltsin's already shaky political position.

French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl have both tried to reassure Yeltsin over the issue during recent visits to Moscow but it remains a key obstacle to improved relations between Russia and the West.

Chirac and Kohl have backed the idea of holding a meeting in the coming months between Russia, the United States, Britain, France and Germany to allow Moscow a chance to discuss NATO's expansion plans.
Such a meeting would precede a scheduled summit of the NATO alliance in July that is expected to formally invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance.

But the United States has responded coolly to the mooted five-power meeting. The issue of NATO's expansion is expected to figure high on the agenda of a planned meeting between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Finland next month.
